slides.title: Diffusion Illusions
slides.speech: Peekaboo optimized a mask through a frozen model. Same loss here, new question: what if we optimize several images at once, and they have to share the same pixels? These are flip illusions. Each square is one image, and as it spins, upside down it becomes a totally different picture. No training at all. Plain Stable Diffusion, frozen.

slides.title: One print, two pictures
slides.speech: Here's one we printed. Right side up, a dog. Rotate the paper 180 degrees, a sloth. The red words are just handwritten labels. The paper is the prime image, the physical thing you hold. Each way of looking at it is an arrangement, a fixed function that has to be differentiable and physically doable. What you see is a derived image, and each one gets its own prompt. So: one prime, two arrangements, identity and rotate 180, dog and sloth.

slides.title: But...how?

elements.text: Score distillation on EACH view, one shared image

slides.speech: But...how? Score distillation, same as Peekaboo, on every derived image. Take the upright view, encode it into Stable Diffusion's latent space, add noise, and the frozen model predicts that noise conditioned on dog. Its prediction error becomes a gradient on that view. Same for the rotated view with sloth. We never backprop through the diffusion U-Net, only through the encoder and the rotation, so both gradients land on the same image and add up. Only the primes get optimized. One detail: each prime is a small Fourier feature network, an MLP from pixel coordinates to color. With raw pixels it hid the second picture in high-frequency noise, and that dies the moment you print it.

slides.title: Stack them

elements.text: Light through two sheets = multiply the colors

slides.speech: Now it gets fun. What else can an arrangement be? Print two images on transparencies and put them on a backlight. The base stays put, the rotator spins on top. Light passes through both sheets, so the color you see is the two colors multiplied. Stacking darkens things, so we scale it up and squash it with a tanh, like a brighter backlight. Multiplication is differentiable too! So two primes, four arrangements, rotator at 0, 90, 180 and 270, four derived images: cat, man, woman, dog. These are photos of the real prints.

slides.title: Hidden overlays

elements.text: Four playgrounds hide a QR code.

slides.speech: Or go further. Four primes, each a playground on its own, so they're also the first four derived images. Stack all four on the light and the product is a fifth image: a QR code that actually scans. That one used a target picture instead of a text prompt. Score distillation alone gives gritty images, so phase two is dream targets. We SDEdit each derived image into a cleaner version, regress the primes toward those targets for about a thousand steps, then make new targets, with the edit strength shrinking each round. Default: 500 score distillation steps, then 8 dream target rounds. Then we print on a regular color laser printer onto transparencies.

slides.title: What became of it

elements.text: “Not good, didn't like it.” — a reviewer
Steve Mould and Matt Parker made videos about it

slides.speech: Does it work beyond cherry-picks? Hidden overlays, PASCAL VOC subjects, four styles, 15 minutes on one A100 each. Honestly, the baseline is SDXL making each of the five images independently, with no illusion constraint, so it measures what the constraint costs. We still beat it on CLIP prompt match, aesthetics, and a new independence score, which checks every image matches its own prompt better than the other four. We only lose on diversity, which makes sense. These are distribution plots, no tables, and no head-to-head with Visual Anagrams, which only does single-image illusions, no overlays. Biggest factor was the prompt, not our method variant. Limits: slow, printer colors shift since we never calibrated, and the hidden image sometimes goes black. One reviewer said, not good, didn't like it. Well...other people did. Best Demo at CVPR 2023, and Steve Mould and Matt Parker made YouTube videos about it. Next: Peekaboo's masks were blobby, and real transparency needs real alpha. MAGICK gets RGBA images by asking the model for green-screen backgrounds.
